insights.title: What the Montgomery ruling changed for broker back offices
insights.excerpt: In May 2026 the US Supreme Court held that state negligent-selection claims against freight brokers are not preempted by federal law. The operational consequence is simple: your vetting file now has to survive being read out loud.
body: On 14 May 2026 the Supreme Court decided Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, holding that state-law negligent-selection claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act. Brokers can now face those claims in state court in circumstances where a preemption defence previously ended the matter early.

We are an operations company, not a law firm, and nothing here is legal advice. Your counsel should tell you what the ruling means for your risk. What we can talk about is the operational consequence, because that is where the work lands.

If a carrier selection decision can be examined years later, the question stops being "did you have a policy?" and becomes "can you show what you did on this particular carrier, on this particular day?" Those are very different requirements. The first needs a document. The second needs a discipline.
A vetting policy nobody can evidence is, in practice, a vetting policy nobody followed.

Most brokers we speak to already have a sound checklist. What they do not always have is proof that the checklist ran identically on the Tuesday afternoon when dispatch was three loads behind and one person was covering two desks.
The check performed, named the same way every time
The source consulted, with a screenshot or export attached
The timestamp, and who performed the check
The result, including the ones that passed unremarkably
The exception path: what failed, who was told, what they decided

That last line matters more than people expect. A file showing that a problem was found, escalated and knowingly accepted by an authorised person tells a much better story than a file with no record of the problem at all.
Why this work suits a supervised desk

Vetting is repetitive, rule-bound and exacting, and it has to happen at the least convenient moments. Those are exactly the conditions under which an in-house team, pressed for time, starts taking shortcuts that nobody intends and nobody notices.

A dedicated desk removes the time pressure from the checklist. The people doing it have no competing dispatch duty, they run the same steps in the same order every time, and a QA reviewer samples their files daily. The broker keeps every approval decision; the desk keeps the record.

Write the checklist down as a numbered procedure, including the escalation path. Decide what evidence each step needs. Then run it on fifty carriers and see whether the files look the same. If they do not, the problem is capacity, and capacity is a solvable problem.
insights.author: Kamship Global

insights.title: Why a freight back office in Nepal works
insights.excerpt: Nepal's time zone covers the US night and the Gulf, European and Asian working day from one centre. That is a real advantage. It is also not the whole story, and it is worth being clear about the trade-offs.
body: Nepal runs at UTC+05:45. Our late evening is the American working day, and our working day covers the Gulf, most of Europe and much of Asia-Pacific. One centre, in one building, under one management structure, can therefore cover a US brokerage night desk and a forwarding day desk without either team working a shift nobody wants.
For a US broker this means the overnight queue is worked by people who are awake, supervised and on their normal schedule, rather than by someone at home fighting sleep.

Around nine in ten of Nepal's IT and outsourcing jobs sit in Kathmandu. Pokhara, the country's second city, has universities, a steady supply of graduates and far less competition for them. In practice that means lower attrition, which for a client translates directly into a team that still knows their process in month nine.
Attrition is the hidden cost of offshore work. A cheap seat that turns over every five months is not cheap; you pay for it in retraining, errors and the quiet erosion of everything you documented.
Where Nepal is not the answer
Licensed work. Customs entries, brokerage authority decisions, legal and tax sign-off must stay with your licensed people. We prepare; we do not file or decide.
Heavy outbound sales calling. Some accents suit some markets. We will tell you plainly if a voice-heavy role is a poor fit rather than sell you seats that disappoint.
Very small volumes. Below about two full-time seats, the supervision and QA structure that makes this work is not worth its overhead to you.
Undefined processes. If the work exists only in one person's head, offshoring it will fail. Document it first; we will help, but it has to happen.

The fair question is whether Nepal can keep the lights on and the internet up. The honest answer is that a centre has to plan for both. Ours runs two independent fibre providers on separate routes and backup power sized for the full floor. Any provider who does not want to discuss this in detail is a provider to avoid.

Dashain and Tihar fall in October and November and matter enormously here. Any serious provider publishes the holiday calendar before you sign and schedules cover in advance. Being surprised by Dashain is a planning failure, not a cultural one.
insights.author: Kamship Global

insights.title: Choosing the first freight process to hand over
insights.excerpt: The first process you outsource decides whether the second one ever happens. Pick for clarity, not for volume, and start smaller than feels worthwhile.
body: The instinct is to hand over the biggest pain first, because that is where the relief would be greatest. The problem is that the biggest pain is usually the messiest process, and messy processes are the ones that fail an offshore handover for reasons that have nothing to do with the team doing them.
Four tests for a good first process
It can be written down. If you can describe it as numbered steps with clear decision rules, it can be taught. If every case is a judgement call, it cannot, yet.
Right and wrong are visible. POD collected or not. Field entered correctly or not. Processes where quality is arguable make a pilot impossible to assess honestly.
It repeats. At least a few dozen times a week, so patterns emerge fast and training pays for itself inside the pilot.
Failure is recoverable. Not the process where one mistake loses the customer. Build trust on ground where an error costs an apology, not an account.

For brokers: POD collection and billing preparation, carrier packet chasing, appointment booking, and documented carrier vetting. For forwarders: job file creation, arrival notices, and milestone updates. These are high volume, checkable, and the cost of a caught error is small.
What usually does not fit first: rate negotiation, customer escalation handling, anything requiring a licence, and anything where the procedure lives in one experienced person's memory.

Two seats on one process for two weeks tells you almost everything you need to know: whether the training holds, whether the QA is real, whether the shift reports are useful, and whether the communication works across the time difference. It costs about the same as a week of a US hire and it is reversible.

The single best predictor of a successful handover is whether the client and the provider wrote the procedure together. Not a provider guessing from a recorded call, and not a client sending a document written for someone who already knows the job. Sit down, walk it through, write it, and argue about the edge cases before they cost anything.

about.h1: A freight back office built in Pokhara
about.lead: Kamship Global is the international operations division of Kamship Pvt Ltd, a Nepali company that also runs the KamShip AI recruitment platform.
body: Offshore freight support has a supervision problem

The usual offering is one person, hired through a marketplace, working alone from home with no team lead, no quality checking, no backup when they are ill and no record of what they did. It is cheap, and it mostly disappoints, and when it disappoints the conclusion drawn is that offshoring does not work for freight.

We think the conclusion is wrong and the structure was the problem. So we built the structure first: a supervised floor, a team lead for every account, a QA reviewer who does not report to that lead, SOPs written with each client, trained backup for every seat, and a written report at the end of every shift.

Freight work is exacting, repetitive and time-critical, which is a hard combination for an in-house team under pressure and a good fit for a desk that does nothing else. It also happens at the wrong hours, and our time zone answers that better than almost anywhere.

Staying in one sector means our three-week training programme can be specific, our SOP library compounds, and a team lead who has seen four hundred carrier files knows what a suspicious one looks like.

Our delivery centre is in Pokhara, Nepal's second city. We recruit from the city's universities and colleges and put every team member through a paid three-week Freight Academy before they touch a client account. Our sister platform, KamShip AI, gives us a large pool of pre-screened candidates across Nepal, which is why our hiring lead times are short.
The centre runs two independent fibre providers on separate routes and backup power sized for the full floor, because a desk that goes dark at 3am is worse than no desk at all.

We publish our prices and our targets. We will not show client logos without written permission or publish testimonials we cannot evidence. If we think a piece of work is a poor fit for our team, we will say so rather than sell you the seats. If a month's quality data is bad, you will see the raw numbers, not a summary of them.
That is not modesty. It is the only way a business whose product is documented, reliable process can credibly sell itself.

why_nepal.lead: A time zone that covers both halves of the working world, a talent pool nobody else is fighting over, and costs that let us charge from $7 an hour without cutting corners on supervision.
body: Nepal runs at UTC+05:45, which is an unusual offset and an unusually useful one. Our evening and night cover the American working day. Our daytime covers the Gulf, most of Europe and much of Asia-Pacific. One centre, one building, one management line, both halves of the clock.
For a US broker this means the overnight queue is worked by people on their normal schedule with a supervisor present, rather than by someone at home at 4am fighting to stay awake.

Roughly nine in ten of Nepal's IT and outsourcing jobs are in Kathmandu. Pokhara has the universities and the graduates but far less competition for them, which shows up in the number that matters most in this business: attrition.

A seat that turns over every five months is not cheap however low the rate. You pay for it in retraining, in errors, and in the quiet erosion of everything you carefully documented. Lower churn is the real product of choosing a second city.

Nepali salaries let us pay above the local market, fund three weeks of training before anyone bills, staff a team lead and a QA reviewer on every account, and still start at $7 an hour. In Manila or Bengaluru the same supervision ratio costs materially more.

The fair question is whether Nepal can keep the lights on and the internet up. A centre has to plan for both, and ours does: two independent fibre providers on separate physical routes, and backup power sized for the full floor rather than for a few desks. Any provider unwilling to discuss this in specifics is one to avoid.

Dashain and Tihar fall in October and November and matter enormously here. We publish the holiday calendar before you sign and schedule cover in advance. Being surprised by Dashain is a planning failure, not a cultural one.
Where Nepal is not the answer

Licensed work stays with your licensed people: we prepare customs entries, we do not file them. Heavy outbound sales calling into some markets is a poor fit and we will say so. Below about two full-time seats the supervision structure costs more than it returns for you. And a process that exists only in one person's head will fail offshore for reasons that have nothing to do with the team receiving it.

security.cert_h2: What we hold, and what we do not
security.cert_p1: We are working toward alignment with ISO/IEC 27001 and will say exactly that until we are certified. We are not certified today, and we will not imply otherwise on a page like this.
security.cert_p2: What we can do now is complete your security questionnaire in full, walk your team through our controls on a call, give you the right to audit them in the agreement, and start with a pilot small enough that the risk is proportionate to what you know about us.
cert_faqs: In your systems. Our staff work inside your TMS, portals and document stores through named accounts. We do not copy client data onto our machines, and local storage and downloads are disabled by configuration, not just by policy.
Yes. The right to audit our controls is written into our standard agreement, and we will host an inspection of the floor with reasonable notice.
What about UK and EU personal data?

We sign a data processing agreement incorporating the UK International Data Transfer Addendum or EU Standard Contractual Clauses before any personal data is shared, and we document the categories of data involved.
What happens when we end the engagement?
A documented offboarding checklist: access revoked within four hours, any client materials returned or destroyed to your instruction, and written confirmation from us that it has been done.
Who is liable if something goes wrong?
Liability is set out in the signed agreement, which your lawyer should review. We carry the obligations we agree to and we will not hide them in a website footnote.

steps.text: We complete an intake questionnaire with you, record a walkthrough of the process, write the SOP together and agree accuracy, turnaround and volume targets in writing. Nothing is hired to the work until this is signed off.

steps.text: You interview and approve the team. Named access with multi-factor sign-in is set up. Week one is 100% quality-checked, with a written report at the end of every shift and a review call on day five while there is still time to change course.

steps.title: Decide — day ten
steps.text: We review the results against the targets with the raw QA data in front of you. Hit them and we continue month to month. Miss them and you walk away, owing nothing beyond the pilot fee.
